Good morning. My name is Marcus Reed and I am the mediator today. Before we start: I am not a judge. I will not decide who is right.
Good morning. I am Ana Tavares and I represent the songwriter, Helena Braga. We came here in good faith.
Thank you. Take three minutes and tell me what happened. Not what you want yet. What happened.
In March the company used one of her songs in a short film. Nobody asked her. She found the film in July, she wrote to them twice, and they have not answered her.
And what is her claim? Give me the number and the thing that is not a number.
A fee for the use, and her name on screen. She has never asked for the film to come down.
Good. Then we already have common ground, and that is more than most rooms start with. If we get to a deadlock on the number, I will stop us and we will come back to it.
That works for us. Before the other side speaks, may I ask you one thing? How long have you been mediating cases like this one?

And you, how long have you worked on cases like this one?

Before we begin, let me tell you what I am and what I am not, because most people who walk into this room expect the wrong thing. They expect me to listen to both sides and then say who is right. That is a judge, and there is a building down the road full of them. I do not decide anything. What I do is help the two of you build an answer that you can both sign, which is a different job and, in my experience, a harder one. There is one rule and it is the only one I will enforce. Nobody interrupts the other side. Not to correct a date, not to say that is not true, not for anything. The first version of a story is the only one that ever comes out whole, and the moment you break it the person stops explaining and starts defending, and we lose the afternoon. And a warning, because I have been doing this for a long time. The people who arrive certain that the case is simple are the ones who take the longest. It is not that they are wrong. It is that they have never had to say the whole story out loud to somebody who was not already on their side, and that turns out to be much harder than anybody expects.

The first time I did a mock mediation in English I wrote my opening statement out, word for word, and learned it. Two hundred and forty words. I was very proud of it. And then the mediator opened with a question I had not prepared for, something about what my client actually wanted, and I could not use a single line of it. So I improvised, and that is when the real problem showed up. Every time I got to a verb I was not sure about, I stopped and rewrote the sentence in my head to go around it. Not out loud. Inside. I would start a sentence about what happened in March, feel the past tense coming, and swap it for something safer and smaller. It cost me the point I was making, and I mean that literally. By the time the sentence came out of my mouth, it said much less than what I meant. Afterwards the woman running the session told me something I still think about. She said, say it wrong and keep going. A wrong verb has never lost anybody an argument. A sentence that stops in the middle loses one every single time. It took me about six months to believe her.

Fewer than five cases in a hundred ever reach a trial, and that figure gets quoted as though it were a scandal. It is read as a failure of the courts, as proof that ordinary people cannot get their day in front of a judge. The people who work inside the system read it almost the opposite way. The number is low because the system is built so that most cases end before that point, and a trial is what happens when everything designed to prevent one has already failed. What changed in the last thirty years is where mediation sits. It used to be something a judge suggested near the end, when the file was thick and everybody was tired. Now the parties do it at the start, and in a growing number of places it is a step you are required to take before a court will even hear you. Not everyone welcomes that. The critics argue that a settlement reached under time pressure is not really a choice. We spoke to a mediator who has worked in commercial disputes for twenty-two years, and her answer was short. The job is not to find the truth, she said. The job is to find the smallest thing both sides can agree on, and build from there.
